notes.meaning: Nahash, king of the Ammonites, marched up and surrounded the town of Jabesh-gilead. The terrified residents offered to surrender peacefully and pay tribute if he would make a treaty with them. Instead of turning to God for help, they gave up too quickly and offered to become servants to an enemy.

Nahash agreed to make a treaty only on one terrible condition: he would gouge out everyone's right eye. Taking their right eye would make them useless as warriors, because in battle a soldier's shield covered his left eye. It was also meant to bring deep shame and disgrace on the entire nation of Israel.

The leaders of Jabesh asked for a seven-day delay so they could send messengers across Israel for help. Nahash arrogantly granted the time, fully confident that no one would dare come to rescue them. The elders promised that if no deliverer appeared by the end of the week, they would surrender.

Messengers arrived at Saul's hometown of Gibeah and told the people about the terrible threat. When the citizens heard the news, they broke down and wept out loud. They cared deeply for their relatives across the river, but they felt completely helpless to save them.

Saul was coming in from the fields behind his plow oxen when he saw the town in tears. Even though he had already been anointed king, he had humbly gone back to ordinary farm work while waiting on God's call. He asked what was troubling everyone, and they told him about the plight of Jabesh.

When Saul heard the report, the Holy Spirit rushed upon him with great power, and he burned with deep anger. His fury was not selfish bad temper, but a righteous anger against cruel injustice. God's Spirit filled him with the courage and zeal needed to act like a true leader.

Saul butchered a pair of oxen and sent the pieces across Israel with an urgent warning. Anyone who refused to march behind Saul and Samuel would have his own cattle cut up in the same way. God placed a holy dread on the people, and the whole nation rallied together as one united army.

Saul gathered the troops at Bezek and counted them, finding three hundred thousand men from Israel and thirty thousand from Judah. Counting the army helped him organize his forces properly for the march. The huge turnout showed how powerfully God had moved the hearts of the people to answer the call.

Saul sent the messengers back with a promise that rescue would arrive by midday tomorrow. When the trapped people of Jabesh received the message, they were filled with joy. Knowing that a rescuer is on the way turns fear into gladness.

The men of Jabesh gave Nahash a clever answer, telling him they would come out to him the next day. They deliberately hid the news of Saul's coming army so the Ammonites would think the city had given up. This trick caused the enemy camp to drop its guard and expect an easy surrender.

Saul divided his troops into three groups and struck the enemy camp just before sunrise. The Israelites caught the Ammonites completely off guard and fought them until the hottest part of the day. The victory was so total that the surviving enemies scattered in every direction, leaving no two together.

After the great victory, the excited people turned to Samuel and remembered the critics who had mocked Saul earlier. Some troublemakers had doubted whether Saul had what it took to lead them. Now the soldiers wanted to drag those men out and execute them for treason.

Saul stepped forward and refused to let anyone be put to death on such a joyful day. He declared that the Lord had brought this great deliverance to Israel, giving God all the credit for the victory. Choosing mercy over revenge helped unite the nation instead of starting a bitter civil feud.

Samuel invited the whole army to travel to Gilgal to renew the kingship. He knew this moment of victory was the best time to bring the nation together in full support of Saul. Gilgal was a historic and holy site, making it the perfect place to dedicate the new kingdom to God.

All the people gathered at Gilgal and publicly confirmed Saul as their king before the Lord. They offered peace offerings, which were sacrifices of thanksgiving and fellowship, sharing a joyful sacred meal together. Saul and all the people celebrated with great gladness because God had given them victory and unity.
